summary: Defines a framework for preconditions in SIP, extensible through IANA registration, and shows how network quality of service can be a precondition for starting a session. Participants reserve network resources before the call proceeds. It does not define new reservation mechanisms. It was later updated by RFCs 4032 and 5027.

plainLanguage.summary: SIP preconditions let the caller and callee describe network requirements before a session starts. The callee can wait to alert the user until all required reservations are ready.

subtitle: A SIP call can wait for required network reservations before alerting the callee.

tldr.problem: A network reservation often needs session details learned during SIP offer and answer. That exchange can alert the callee before the reservation is ready.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC adds current, desired, and confirmation status attributes to SDP. User agents pause session establishment until the mandatory resource conditions are met.
tldr.outcome: The framework lets a session wait for existing reservation mechanisms; it does not define a new way to reserve resources. RFC 3312 was updated by RFC 4032 and RFC 5027.

today: RFC 3312 is a Proposed Standard and has been updated by RFC 4032 and RFC 5027. Read those documents with this framework.

sections.title: Why a Call Can Wait Before Ringing
sections.content:
Some systems want network resources reserved before the callee is alerted. Yet the reservation may require the callee's address, port, and session parameters, which become available through the initial Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) offer and answer. The Session Description Protocol (SDP) carries the session details.

RFC 3312 addresses this conflict with a precondition: a constraint placed in the offer. The recipient answers, but pauses session establishment until the conditions are met. The RFC defines quality-of-service (QoS) preconditions; it does not define a new reservation mechanism.
sections.plainLanguage: The caller may need the callee's session details before the network can reserve resources. A precondition lets the call exchange those details while delaying the alert until the required reservation is ready.

sections.title: Current Status and Desired Status
sections.content:
For each media stream, the user agents track the current status of resource reservations and the desired status required before the session continues. The desired status acts as a threshold: establishment resumes when current status reaches or exceeds it.

For example, a reservation in the send direction does not meet a requirement for both send and receive directions. The RFC's basic call flow uses an INVITE offer, a 183 Session Progress answer, resource reservation, an UPDATE with new status, and then a ringing response after the mandatory conditions are met.
sections.plainLanguage: Current status reports what the network has reserved. Desired status reports what the session needs, and the call waits until the current status is sufficient.

sections.title: The SDP Preconditions
sections.content:
The RFC defines three media-level SDP attributes: a=curr reports current status, a=des states the desired status, and a=conf asks for confirmation when a threshold is reached. This document defines the qos precondition type.

Status can be end-to-end (e2e) or segmented between local and remote access networks. Direction tags are none, send, recv, and sendrecv. A desired-status line also carries a strength: none, optional, or mandatory; refusal descriptions can use failure or unknown.

The tags describe the point of view of the SDP author. Thus, send points from offerer to answerer in an offer, and from answerer to offerer in an answer. QoS means quality of service.
sections.plainLanguage: The SDP attributes report what is ready, what must be ready, and when the other side should be told about a change. Direction labels are interpreted from the point of view of the person who wrote that SDP.

sections.title: How Offers and Answers Agree on Status
sections.content:
Each user agent keeps a local status table, while an offer and answer use a transaction table to exchange a shared view. The answerer updates information that is out of date and returns the result; the RFC describes this as a model of behavior, not a required software design.

The answerer may raise a desired strength but must not lower it. none means no reservation is needed, optional means the agents should try but may continue without it, and mandatory means the session must not continue unless the reservation is provided. Direction and local/remote tags are inverted in the answer.
sections.plainLanguage: The offer and answer let both user agents agree on the current reservation state and the required level. The answerer may ask for a stronger reservation, but cannot weaken a requirement from the offer.

sections.title: Pausing, Resuming, and Confirming
sections.content:
A user agent server that receives preconditions should not alert the user until every mandatory condition is met. While establishment is paused, user agents should not send media data; for the Real-time Transport Protocol (RTP), this means sending neither RTP nor RTCP packets. When a server cannot meet a mandatory condition on its own, it includes a confirmation-status attribute so its peer can send an updated offer when the threshold is reached.

The same pause applies to changes during an existing session: both sides should keep using the old session parameters until the mandatory conditions for the new parameters are met. Preconditions are signaled in SDP, and an offer with any mandatory precondition must use the precondition option tag in a Require header. A user agent using preconditions must support PRACK and UPDATE.
sections.plainLanguage: The callee waits to alert the user, and the participants wait to switch session settings, until required reservations are ready. A confirmation attribute tells the other side when it should receive an updated status.

sections.title: When a Precondition Cannot Be Met
sections.content:
The RFC adds SIP status code 580, Precondition Failure. An answerer that cannot or will not meet the conditions should reject the offer with this response. If an unacceptable offer arrives in a response and SIP cannot reject it directly, the receiver answers and then sends CANCEL or BYE as appropriate.

A failure description identifies the desired status that caused the refusal. An unknown mandatory precondition type must also be refused, except when the only unknown mandatory conditions are tagged local. The refusal uses the unknown strength tag for that case.
sections.plainLanguage: If a required condition cannot be met, the user agent can reject the offer and identify the condition that failed. An unknown mandatory condition is also refused unless it concerns only the receiver's local network.

sections.title: Integrity and Authentication
sections.content:
A party between the user agents could add desired-status attributes to prevent a session from proceeding, or change current-status values so a session starts before its conditions are met. The RFC says integrity protection can prevent these changes.

An unauthenticated request that triggers resource reservations can expose the reserver to denial of service. Requests that contain preconditions should therefore be authenticated. The RFC registers the SDP attributes, status code, option tag, and the qos precondition type.
sections.plainLanguage: A message intermediary could change the stated requirements or falsely report that they are met. Integrity protection and authentication help prevent those attacks and misuse of reservation resources.
